Q489.L1t: Spacecraft from several nations have been sent to explore many bodies across the solar system.
Q489.L2t: Both the Soviet Union and the United States have made soft landings on other solid worlds.

Q506.L1t: The Vietnam War was a long conflict in Southeast Asia in which American forces became deeply involved.
Q506.L2t: Gallup and other pollsters regularly asked Americans about the Vietnam War through the 1960s, and opinion shifted over time.
Q506.L3t: In 1965 the public still largely rallied behind the president's decision to escalate, so only a minority regarded the deployment as an error.
Q506.L4t: Only about one in four Americans thought sending troops was a mistake.
Q506.L2f: Gallup did not begin asking Americans about Vietnam until the mid-1970s.
Q506.L3f: By 1965 opposition to the deployment was already overwhelming, with the great majority of Americans calling it an error.
Q506.L4f: The vast majority, roughly five in six Americans, thought sending troops to Vietnam was a mistake.

Q216.L1t: Many organizations spent heavily around 1999 preparing their computer systems for the new year.
Q216.L2t: The Y2K problem arose because many older systems stored years using only two digits.
Q216.L3t: The letter is the standard abbreviation for the metric prefix kilo, as in kilometre, so the phrase simply means year 2000.
Q216.L4t: The K stands for a thousand, the number the metric prefix kilo represents.
Q216.L2f: The term Y2K was first coined in 1985 by a British government minister.
Q216.L3f: In computing shorthand, a trailing K abbreviates the programming source behind a bug, and Y2K named the faulty year-handling software.
Q216.L4f: The K stands for computer code.
